title: Seminar 12 · Tests of dependence: contingency, ANOVA, correlation, regression, trend
intro: Same five steps as Seminar 11: H0 and H1 → test statistic and its distribution → value of the test statistic → rejection region from the tables → conclusion in words. Data from the Excel file are shown as tables. Test statistics and critical values were calculated for this app (the file shows them as equations that could not be copied); every conclusion matches the one in the file.

exercises.text: During the efficiency verification of four methods (B1, B2, B3, B4) that were employed to increase the labour productivity (an increase being expressed by numbers from 1-lowest to 5-highest), 220 employees of a particular company were randomly selected from a population of all employees, the following data being collected:
exercises.after: Assume all the expected frequencies to be large enough and at a 5 % significance level, carry out a statistical hypothesis test to judge if the increase in productivity depends on the method.

parts.q: Value of the test statistic g

options: Reject H0: productivity increase depends on the method
Do not reject H0: productivity increase and method are independent
parts.model: At a 5% significance level, the value of the test statistic is not inconsistent with H0 that the productivity increase and method are independent.

exercises.text: The following contingency table contains data on the education of randomly selected readers of three different magazines (A, B, C). Assuming all the expected frequencies are large enough, at a 0.5% significance level run a statistical hypothesis test to judge whether the selection of a magazine depends on the education attained.

parts.q: Value of the test statistic g

options: Reject H0: the selection of a magazine depends on education
Do not reject H0: they are independent
parts.model: At a 0.5% significance level, the value of the test statistic is inconsistent with H0 in favour of H1 that the selection of a magazine depends on the education attained.

exercises.text: The data on the “Exercise_ctt3“ sheet are a random sample from the population of all people in a specific region in the Czech Republic. Use the data to carry out a statistical hypothesis test (at a 7% significance level, under the assumption of all expected frequencies being large enough) to judge whether the willingness to move to another city (1=strong agreement, 2=agreement, 3=I don’t care, 4=disagreement, 5=strong disagreement) depends on the gender (1=male, 2=female).

table.caption: The 275 rows of the Excel sheet, counted into a contingency table:
head: Willingness
Male (1)
Female (2)

parts.q: Value of the test statistic g

options: Reject H0: willingness to move depends on gender
Do not reject H0: they are independent
parts.model: At a 7% significance level, the value of the test statistic is inconsistent with the null hypothesis in favour of the alternative hypothesis that the willingness to move to another city depends on the gender.

exercises.text: A contingency table was constructed for a data set of 110 randomly selected university staff in the Czech Republic, the variables of interest being a teaching degree and the gender. In the contingency table below, the observed frequencies (upper ones) and some expected frequencies (expected in the case of independence) are available (you need to determine 4 missing expected frequencies). Round the results off to one decimal place. Assume all the expected frequencies to be large enough and run a statistical hypothesis test (at an 11% significance level) to assess if there is a relationship between gender and pedagogical degree.

table.caption: Contingency table of Gender and Degree (observed / expected)
head: Junior assistant
Senior assistant
Senior lecturer
Professor
Total

parts.q: Value of the test statistic g

options: Reject H0: gender and degree are related
Do not reject H0: gender and degree are independent
parts.model: At an 11% significance level, the value of the test statistic is not inconsistent with H0 that the gender and pedagogical degree are independent. Be careful with such a strong rounding as it may influence your results a lot!

exercises.text: The following contingency table contains data on the general knowledge of the European Union (1=I know nothing, 2=I know only a little, 3=I know quite a lot, 4=I know a lot) and the age of randomly selected respondents (1=the youngest, …, 5=the oldest) in Prague. Under the assumption of all expected frequencies being large enough, perform a statistical hypothesis test (at a 10% significance level) to judge if there is a relationship between the level of knowledge and age. Are the conditions for a justified employment of the test fulfilled?

parts.q: Value of the test statistic g

options: Reject H0: knowledge depends on age
Do not reject H0: knowledge and age are independent

parts.q: Are the conditions for a justified employment of the test fulfilled?
parts.model: At a 10% significance level, the value of the test statistic is not inconsistent with H0 that the level of knowledge and age are independent. Some of the expected frequencies are pretty low (the smallest is about 3.2), fulfilment of the conditions thus being very questionable, the test seems not to be justified.

exercises.text: In the case of contingency tables with insufficiently occupied cells (low expected frequencies), it is often recommended to combine the categories. Use the contingency table from the previous exercise combining the first three age categories into “younger person“ and the remaining two into “older person“ categories. Explore how this action may influence the results of the independence test.

head: Level of knowledge
Younger (1–3)
Older (4–5)

parts.q: Value of the test statistic g

options: Reject H0
Do not reject H0: knowledge and age are independent
parts.model: At a 10% significance level, the value of the test statistic is not inconsistent with H0 that the level of knowledge and age are independent.

exercises.text: Assume the expected frequencies to be large enough and use a statistical hypothesis test (at a 3% significance level) to evaluate a research hypothesis about independence between gender and the preferred place to live using data of 514 randomly selected people.

exercises.text: The marketing agency conducted a survey of annual household expenditure (per one household member) in a city. exercises.after: At a 5% significance level, run a statistical hypothesis test to judge whether the expenditure depend on the type of household.

parts.q: H0: μ1 = μ2 = μ3. What is H1?
options: non H0: at least one population mean differs
parts.model: Note there are three populations (and their parameters) of interest. H1: non H0, i.e. at least one population mean differs, i.e. household expenditure and the type of household are dependent.

The table below indicates the results of one-way ANOVA in Excel. Use a statistical hypothesis test procedure at a 5% significance level to judge whether the mean expenditure values differ for the households with different numbers of members.

options: Reject H0: mean expenditure differs
Do not reject H0: expenditure and number of members are independent
parts.model: f = 2.59 < 3.49 (and P-value 0.1013 > 0.05): at a 5% significance level, the value of the test statistic is not inconsistent with H0 that the expenditures and the number of household members are independent.

The table below presents the numbers of words of the same text they could type in 10 minutes. At a 5% significance level, carry out a statistical hypothesis test to judge if the means of words typed on the keyboards of different brands differ.

parts.q: Value of the test statistic f

options: Reject H0: the means differ by keyboard brand
Do not reject H0

exercises.after: Use the above results to carry out a statistical hypothesis test (at a 5% significance level) of the independence between the travel time and the selected route.

exercises.text: When looking for an appropriate chocolate packaging technology, an experiment was done. 12 randomly selected employees of a chocolate factory who took part in it were randomly divided into 4 equal groups. Each group having tested a different technology, the number of packaged chocolates per hour was recorded. Fill in the missing values into the table below and perform a statistical hypothesis test (at a 5% significance level) to assess whether different technologies bring different results.

options: Reject H0: technologies bring different results
Do not reject H0
parts.model: At a 5% significance level, the value of the test statistic is inconsistent with the null hypothesis in favour of the alternative hypothesis that the number of packaged chocolates per hour and the packaging technology are dependent.

exercises.text: There are data about the results (in points) of 8 randomly chosen students in two mid-term tests on the “Exercise_cor1“ sheet. At a 4% significance level, carry out a hypothesis test to explore a research hypothesis that the points gained in test1 and points gained in test2 are linearly independent.

parts.q: Value of the test statistic t

options: Reject H0: the points are correlated
Do not reject H0: the points are linearly independent
parts.model: H0: ρXY = 0, H1: ρXY ≠ 0. At a 4% significance level, the value of the test statistic is not inconsistent with H0 that the points gained in test1 and points gained in test2 are linearly independent.

exercises.text: There are data on randomly selected countries (a random sample from the population of all countries) – namely the number of private cars, GDP in dollars and the number of kilometres travelled by trains and buses (all counted relative to one inhabitant) – on the “Exercise_cor2“ sheet. For each pair of variables, perform a statistical hypothesis test to judge, whether the variables are correlated.

parts.q: Cars and GDP: correlation coefficient r
Cars and GDP: value of the test statistic t
Cars and trains & buses: value of the test statistic t
GDP and trains & buses: value of the test statistic t
Conclusion at a 5% significance level (critical value t0.975(17) = 2.110)
options: All three pairs are correlated (reject H0 each time)
Only cars and GDP are correlated
No pair is correlated
parts.model: All three values |t| are at least 2.110, so for each pair the value of the test statistic is inconsistent with H0 in favour of H1 that the variables are correlated.

b) Judge the quality of the regression model using the coefficient of determination. r² =

parts.model: About 94.9 % of the variability of the achieved scores is explained by the regression line (by the preparation time). The model fits the data very well.

parts.q: c) At a 1% significance level, test the slope. s(b1) from Excel = 0.0790. Value of the test statistic t

Do not reject H0: no linear relationship
